targets.approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north to Burlington, then WA-20 east through Marblemount, and turn onto Cascade River Road, following its paved-then-gravel surface about 21.7 miles to a small pullout at 3,200 ft that marks the unmaintained Boston Basin Trailhead (a different stop, a couple of miles up-road of the Eldorado trailhead, and just before the road's end at Cascade Pass). From there a steep, unmaintained climbers' path follows the old Diamond Mine roadbed briefly before climbing hard, crossing several streams, and breaking above treeline (~5,300 ft) to reach the popular Boston Basin high camp around 6,400 ft — roughly 3-4 miles one-way with about 3,000-3,300 ft of elevation gain. From camp, West Ridge climbers continue cross-country over the glacier to a couloir that gains the ridge crest. Because Boston Basin is a high-demand cross-country camping zone in North Cascades National Park, overnight parties need a wilderness permit; a portion of peak-season (mid-May to mid-October) slots can be reserved in advance via Recreation.gov's early-access lottery, with the remainder issued as limited first-come, first-served walk-up permits. For this specific route: from Boston Basin high camp, a short approach up into the Forbidden Peak zone reaches this minor summit; North and South Ridge differ only in which side of the formation is climbed from the same camp.
targets.descent: Descend the North Ridge: one short rappel from fixed slings, then reverse that ridge.
targets.descent_text: Descend the North Ridge: make one rappel of about 40 ft from fixed slings, then downclimb the rest of that ridge and return to camp.

targets.descent: Descend via the north side towers, reversing rappels between towers; alternatively downclimb to the notch system used on ascent.

targets.approach: Approach as for the East Ridge/Hardscrabble Route: walk/bike the gated Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road to the Hardscrabble Lakes boot path, then continue to lower Hardscrabble Lake. Traverse the lake's left (north) side and scramble two rock bands to reach the buttress's south side at roughly 5,400 ft.

targets.approach: From the Dingford Creek gate, walk or bike the closed Middle Fork road (FR 56) about 7.7 miles to its end at Hardscrabble Horse Camp; bikes go no farther. Burnt Boot stands across the Middle Fork to the south, and its north ridge drops straight from the summit to the river near 3,100 ft. There is no bridge here (the next one is at Pedro Camp, near mile 13), so head upstream from the horse camp toward Hardscrabble Creek and ford the river; it can run cold and thigh-deep in July, and logs across it may not reach. From the south bank it is cross-country up steep forest and brush on the ridge to the base of its steepest granite, where the roped climbing starts. There is no trail or established line off the valley floor.
targets.name: North Ridge
targets.previous_skip_reason: no source found for the roped North Ridge descent; the sibling descent is for a different, scrambling line

targets.approach: Reached via the North Fork Entiat Trail to Saska Basin and Saska Pass, commonly combined with ascents of Saska Peak, Emerald Peak, and Pinnacle Mountain on the same trip rather than as a dedicated single-peak approach.
targets.descent: Reverse the ridge/couloir, or descend the east/southeast slopes if that side was used to finish the climb.

targets.approach: The line most often written up starts on the Monument 78 Trail in Manning Park, BC and crosses the US/Canada border in the boundary clearing south of Castle Creek; entering the US on foot away from a port of entry is not lawful, so the lawful way in is the long walk north on the PCT from Harts Pass to Castle Pass at the head of Castle Creek. As written up, the Canadian line continues: Cross the Castle Creek bridge, push south through brush and downed timber, navigate the boundary clearing and wetland openings, then follow Castle Creek uphill from about 4,500 ft through alder terrain to a camp around 5,500 ft in Castle Creek Basin.
targets.descent: Reverse the ascent line back through the notch, northeast gully and south gully to Castle Creek Basin camp.
targets.name: South Route
targets.previous_skip_reason: no source found to thicken the descent beyond what is stored

wa_american_border_peak_southeast_face.approach: Start at the Twin Lakes trailhead (~5,200 ft), the rough, rutted end of Twin Lakes Road (many parties park short and walk the final rutted miles, as the road note indicates). From the parking area pick up the signed High Pass Trail; at about a quarter mile it splits from the short spur up Winchester Mountain Lookout — stay left/north on the High Pass Trail. The trail contours along the west side of Winchester Mountain, dips across an unnamed minor saddle often called Low Pass (open views west to Tomyhoi Peak), then climbs steadily to High Pass itself (~5,960 ft, roughly 2 miles and about 750 ft of gain from the trailhead), where Mount Baker comes into view to the south. At High Pass, leave the maintained tread and follow the climbers' path north and west down to the old Gargett Mine workings (~5,400 ft) — the mine creek is the last reliable water source until you reach lingering snow patches high on the peak. From the mine, traverse north and contour onto Mount Larrabee's southwest and west flanks: this is a long, unmarked, exposed sidehill (well over a mile) across steep talus, scree, heather, and brush, aiming for a notch around 6,200-6,300 ft on Larrabee's northwest rib. Drop sl
wa_american_border_peak_southeast_face.descent_text: Descend by reversing the Southeast Face/South Ridge line back down to the South AmBo Saddle — the terrain is loose and complex enough that there is no clean walk-off alternative. Expect two to four short rappels through the summit chimney/gully system, with the count depending on party size, rope handling, and which chockstone squeeze you take: the standard, recommended line threads the low "keyhole"/tunnel beneath a large chockstone (pull packs off, push them through, crawl after), giving a clean, low-angle rappel; parties who instead rig over the lip of the chockstone get a harder, overhanging drop and sometimes add an extra rappel to manage it. A single 60m rope, doubled, is sufficient for the individual rappels (each reported at around 75 ft/~23 m), so plan on doubled-strand rappels off a 60m rope rather than needing two ropes. Anchors are entirely natural — slung chockstones and horns with in-place webbing that is often sun-bleached and aged — there are no bolts on this route, so inspect and back up (or replace) any tat you find and carry your own cord/rap rings; at least one party describes sacrificing a rope that got stuck in a rappel crack, so a pull-cord or a stuck-rope co
wa_american_border_peak_southeast_face.name: Southeast Face / South Ridge

wa_bald_eagle_peak_scramble.approach: From the pullout along FR 6835 (West Fork Foss Road) — just past the concrete bridge over the East Fork Foss River, about half a mile from its junction with FR 68 and roughly 5.2 miles from US-2 at Skykomish — there is no maintained trail. Climbers cross to the north side of the road and pick up the toe of Bald Eagle's north ridge at about 1,600 ft, entering second-growth forest thick with fallen timber that requires weaving/scrambling over deadfall for the first few hundred feet of gain. Stay on or near the ridge crest heading south-southeast; around 2,600 ft the forest transitions to older growth and the underbrush thins out, making travel noticeably easier and the ridgeline easy to follow with few reasons to leave it. The going stays moderate until roughly 4,500 ft, where the ridge narrows and steepens into the trip's brushiest stretch — a pointier crest with real drop-offs on both sides, dense small trees/slide alder crowding the tread, and (in season) heavy mosquito pressure; move carefully here as exposure picks up. By 5,200 ft the ridge opens into rockier, more open terrain, with snow patches lingering later into the season (more persistent on the east side of the crest than
wa_bald_eagle_peak_scramble.descent_text: This is a walk-off/downclimb — descend by reversing the North Ridge exactly as ascended; there is no rappelling on the standard route. From the summit, downclimb the steep snow/small-tree section back to the top of the 5,400 ft cliff band, then carefully reverse the rising traverse and gully bypass on the east side of the crest to regain the ridge crest below the cliffs — this bypass is the one spot demanding real route-finding and careful downclimbing (loose rock and exposure in the gully), so many parties down-face here rather than walk it. Below 5,200 ft, follow the open rocky ridge back into the brushy, exposed 4,500-5,200 ft stretch, staying on the crest to avoid the steep drop-offs to either side. Once back into old-growth forest below 4,500 ft the ridge broadens and travel gets easy and fast; one party found the descent takes well under half the time of the ascent once past the brush and cliff band. Continue down through the second-growth/deadfall lower forest to regain FR 6835 at the East Fork Foss River bridge pullout. No technical anchors (bolted or natural) are used on this route — it is entirely natural terrain.
wa_bald_eagle_peak_scramble.name: Standard Scramble

wa_big_chiwaukum_west_ridge.approach: From the Whitepine Creek Trailhead (about 2,800 ft), follow Whitepine Creek Trail #1582 up the valley for about 2.5 miles to the junction with Wildhorse Creek Trail #1592. Bear left onto the Wildhorse Creek Trail and climb through forest into the Wildhorse basin to about 5,400 ft, where the trail passes directly west of the summit. Leave the trail here.
wa_big_chiwaukum_west_ridge.descent_text: Reverse the route: down the summit ledges to below the headwall, back west along the west ridge, then down through the meadows to rejoin the Wildhorse Creek Trail, and out the Whitepine Creek Trail to the car.
wa_big_chiwaukum_west_ridge.name: West Ridge via Wildhorse Creek

wa_big_four_mountain_dry_creek_route.approach: From the Big Four Picnic Area / Ice Caves Trailhead (1,640 ft) on the Mountain Loop Highway, follow the paved nature-trail toward the ice caves, then leave the trail to cross the South Fork Stillaguamish River on a fallen log. Travel southeasterly through open forest roughly a mile to reach Dry Creek, then ascend through the lower basin -- in snow conditions via a hidden snow chute, in bare conditions via a series of class 3-4 ledges and ramps -- into the upper basin. From the upper basin, climb the steep main couloir, then traverse the exposed red slabs to gain the summit ridge.
wa_big_four_mountain_dry_creek_route.descent_text: Most parties descend the same Dry Creek line they climbed. From the true summit, reverse the summit ridge over the lower (first) bump, then set up a roughly 60-meter rappel from a notch on the south ridge -- some parties have found a 60m rope barely reaches the anchor/chockstone. Below the rappel, bypass steep snow and waterfall-moistened rock to the side, then downclimb roughly two more rope-lengths of steep terrain to regain the lower basin before retracing the approach back across the South Fork Stillaguamish and out to the trailhead. In winter/spring, parties instead downclimb the Dry Creek couloir itself, which parties describe as a genuinely dangerous, insecure downclimb.
wa_big_four_mountain_dry_creek_route.name: Dry Creek Route

wa_big_four_mountain_spindrift_couloir.approach: Walk the nearly wheelchair-accessible nature trail from the Big Four Picnic Area toward the Ice Caves, to the open basin below the North Face. From the trail's end, move right to find a break in the lower cliffs -- straightforward with adequate snow cover, but may require bushwhacking on the far right in sparse-snow years.
wa_big_four_mountain_spindrift_couloir.descent_text: The route tops out on the summit ridge well west of the true summit. Descent goes northwest, via rappels and steep downclimbing, to the col between Big Four and Hall Peak; from there, multiple tree-anchored rappels lead back down through the North Face bowl to the base of the face. Careful navigation is essential -- parties have mistakenly descended south instead of northwest in poor visibility.
wa_big_four_mountain_spindrift_couloir.name: Spindrift Couloir

wa_big_snow_mountain_east_ridge_hardscra.approach: Start at the Dingford Creek Trailhead gate and walk (or mountain-bike) the closed Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road about 7 miles to the boot path for Hardscrabble Lakes, which starts roughly half a mile short of the old Hardscrabble Horse Camp, across the road from a large fallen log. Follow the climbers path east through forest to upper Hardscrabble Lake, staying near the inlet — straying left leads into cliff bands.
wa_big_snow_mountain_east_ridge_hardscra.descent_text: From the summit, retrace the east ridge onto the north-slope granite slab, climb back up to the col, and descend the gully to upper Hardscrabble Lake; follow the inlet-side climbers path back down to the lower lake and rejoin the old road for the multi-mile walk-out.
wa_big_snow_mountain_east_ridge_hardscra.name: East Ridge (Hardscrabble) Route

wa_big_snow_mountain_north_slope_dingfor.approach: Drive to the Dingford Creek Trailhead gate via Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Rd / FSR 56 (about 18 mi from North Bend; the last several miles are rough gravel, high-clearance recommended). Hike the Dingford Creek Trail roughly 3.2 mi to the Hester Lake Trail junction, continue left (east) toward Myrtle Lake (about 2 more miles). From Myrtle Lake, leave the trail and climb steep, increasingly brushy terrain toward Big Snow Lake, then traverse right around Snowflake Lake before ascending gullies/a snow couloir on the mountain's NW flank to the upper rock fields.
wa_big_snow_mountain_north_slope_dingfor.descent_text: Downclimb the same chutes/couloir used on ascent, taking care on crumbly, mossy rock and any residual snow or ice, especially early in the season; traverse back around Snowflake Lake, drop to Big Snow Lake, then pick a line down through brush to Myrtle Lake and follow the Dingford Creek Trail out to the trailhead.
wa_big_snow_mountain_north_slope_dingfor.name: North Slope (Dingford) Route

wa_black_peak_northeast_ridge.approach: As for the South Ridge: Rainy Pass/Lake Ann trailhead on SR-20, via Heather Pass and Lewis Lake to a camp at Wing Lake (~6,900 ft). From camp, ascend snow (a small permanent snowfield/mini-glacier can persist below the col into September) toward the low point in the Northeast Ridge — following the hogsback moraine wide right and then traversing back left to the notch is reported to stay on more stable ground than a direct line.
wa_black_peak_northeast_ridge.descent_text: From the summit, work down and south toward the South Ridge route, using one rappel or a down-climb to get below the initial band of rock, then continuing south to the south col. From there the descent follows the South Ridge's loose, cairned gully (described by multiple parties as tedious and 'choss'-prone) back down to snow slopes and Wing Lake. Some parties glissade the snow lower down early in the season.
wa_black_peak_northeast_ridge.name: Northeast Ridge

wa_north_ridge_7.approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north to Burlington, then WA-20 east through Marblemount, and turn onto Cascade River Road, following its paved-then-gravel surface about 21.7 miles to a small pullout at 3,200 ft that marks the unmaintained Boston Basin Trailhead (a different stop from the Eldorado trailhead about 2.5 miles down-road, and just before the road's end at Cascade Pass). From there a steep, unmaintained climbers' path follows the old Diamond Mine roadbed briefly before climbing hard, crossing several streams, and breaking above treeline (~5,300 ft) to reach the popular Boston Basin high camp around 6,400 ft — roughly 3-4 miles one-way with about 3,000-3,300 ft of elevation gain. From camp, West Ridge climbers continue cross-country over the glacier to a couloir that gains the ridge crest. Because Boston Basin is a high-demand cross-country camping zone in North Cascades National Park, overnight parties need a wilderness permit; a portion of peak-season (mid-May to mid-October) slots can be reserved in advance via Recreation.gov's early-access lottery, with the remainder issued as limited first-come, first-served walk-up permits. For this specific route: from Boston Basin high ca
wa_north_ridge_7.descent_text: From tower summit, establish anchor and rappel 40 feet. Reverse fourth-class scrambling pitches and traverse back toward notch before descending to camp.
wa_north_ridge_7.name: North Ridge

wa_south_ridge_3.approach: Start at the Rainy Pass Picnic Area/Lake Ann trailhead on SR 20 (milepost ~157.5, elev. ~4,850 ft; 40-car lot with privy). Follow the Lake Ann/Maple Pass Trail (#740) about 1-1.5 miles to a signed junction and take the right fork toward Heather Pass (the left fork is the spur to Lake Ann). Climb through meadows to Heather Pass (~2.6 mi, ~6,100 ft), where the maintained trail ends. From the pass, pick up the unmarked climbers' path heading north, crossing two talus/boulder fields before dropping to Lewis Lake (~3.5-4 mi, ~5,700 ft; timbered campsites on the north side, water available) — this off-trail stretch is the main route-finding challenge of the approach, especially with cairns buried by early-season snow. From Lewis Lake, climb roughly 1,200 ft more of meadow and talus to Wing Lake (~5 mi, ~6,900 ft), the standard base camp, with sites in the trees on the right as you reach the lake and reliable water into late summer. From Wing Lake, go around the right (north) side of the lake and aim for the obvious talus/snow gully leading into the couloir just south of the summit; climb this gully, then angle climber's-right out of it to avoid cliff bands directly below the col, topping
wa_south_ridge_3.descent_text: This is the standard descent line for the peak — no separate down-route to learn. The ascent from the south col follows the cairned ridge (some class 3 moves) and a loose gully just west of the crest to the summit pyramid; the final section is a cairned class 2 ledge system traversing below the summit block that is exposed near its end, followed by a short (~15 ft) class 4 step to the true summit. On the way down, reverse this: downclimb the class 4 step (a boulder slung here permits a short optional rappel or hand-line — a single 30m rope is more than enough rope, and many parties skip the rope and downclimb it facing in), reverse the ledge traverse and the gully, and retrace the ridge back to the south col. From the col, descend the scree-and-snow slope (glissade-able early season) back down to Wing Lake, then hike out the approach trail. There is no mandatory multi-pitch rappel sequence on this route; the class 4 summit step is the only spot where climbers occasionally use a rope on the way down.
wa_south_ridge_3.name: South Ridge

wa_bryant_peak_southeast_slopes.approach: From I-90 Exit 47, take Denny Creek Road (FR 58) about 3 miles, past Denny Creek Campground, then turn left onto FR 5830 to the Denny Creek trailhead (~2,300 ft). Follow the Denny Creek Trail (#1014, the Melakwa Lake trail) up the valley past waterfalls, then up steeper switchbacks to Hemlock Pass, about 4 miles and roughly 2,300 ft above the car. At the crest of the pass turn right and follow the ridge on a bearing of about 33°, skirting cliff bands mainly on the left, to a plateau and meadow on the ridge. Early in the season, while snow still covers the brush, a brushy notch behind trees on the right leads about 170 ft up and then northeast to a meadow at the foot of the talus field that wraps about three-quarters of the peak's base; later in the season that line is choked with brush, so stay on the ridge and go straight up it to the summit block. The final scramble is loose rock on the left, or when snow-free around the exposed north side; helmets are recommended. The round trip is about 9 miles with roughly 3,600 ft of gain for Bryant alone; adding nearby Hemlock Peak makes it about 9.5 miles and 3,900 ft.
wa_bryant_peak_southeast_slopes.descent_text: This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble with no rappels and no fixed anchors. Reverse the ascent: downclimb the loose Class 3 summit block carefully, facing in where it is steep, then return across the talus and down the ridge to Hemlock Pass, keeping to the ascent line around the cliff bands rather than cutting down the fall line. From the pass, follow the Denny Creek Trail back down to the trailhead. The steep gully between Bryant and Chair Peak on the Source Lake side is a separate line and an avalanche path in winter and spring; it is not a descent from this route.
wa_bryant_peak_southeast_slopes.name: Southwest Ridge (Hemlock Pass)

wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.approach: Park at the Dingford Creek Trailhead, where Middle Fork Snoqualmie Road (FS Road 56) is gated to vehicles — the last few miles of FS 56 are pitted with potholes and washboard, so high-clearance is strongly recommended — then walk or bike about 7.5 mi of closed road to its old end at the former Dutch Miller Gap Trailhead (Trail #1030). Do not follow the maintained Dutch Miller Gap trail; instead ford the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River roughly 300 ft upstream of the trailhead to its true-right (north) bank. Early-season and post-snowmelt (roughly June) this ford can run thigh-deep and cold — scout upstream for a braided or log crossing if flows are high. Once across, climb the boulder/talus field directly above the river for about 400 vertical feet until you hit a rock band. At the cliff, angle left (west) into a brushy gully thick with salmonberry and black currant — expect real bushwhacking here, not a trail. Follow the gully up into timber around 3,900 ft, then traverse upward through the trees until you break out onto open talus. From the talus, work up and climber's-left toward the low notch/pass beside Point 5,841, which separates Burnt Boot's summit block from the peak immediate
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the short class 3–4 ridge step off the summit block back to the Point 5,841 pass, then descend the steep snow ramp below it facing in, plunge-stepping or self-belaying with an ice axe (a controlled glissade may be possible lower down if the snow is soft and the runout is clean and known — check before committing). From the base of the ramp, work back down through talus and boulders, staying climber's-right where possible to avoid the loosest scree, drop into the timber, and downclimb the brushy salmonberry/currant gully back to the cliff band. Pick a descending line through the boulder field to the river and re-ford to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb — there is no fixed rappel station or bolted anchor on this route, and the discipline (scrambling, not roped climbing) is consistent with that. In icy or wet conditions some parties might choose to build a single natural rappel (sling around a horn or tree) to protect the short class 4 step just above the pass, but that is a judgment call, not standard practice for the route. Note there is a separate, much harder roped North Ridge line on this peak (1971 first ascent by Williamson/Oas/Buch
wa_burnt_boot_peak_north_route.name: North Route

wa_cardinal_peak_se_slopes.approach: From the end of FR-5606 (the North Fork Entiat Trailhead, ~3,940 ft), pick up the North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437. This lower section sits outside wilderness, so mountain bikes are legal and commonly used to knock out easy miles. The first ~6 miles follow the North Fork Entiat River on a gentle, mostly forested grade, with the river itself as a reliable water source the whole way — top off here, since the route runs dry above. Some post-wildfire sections have significant blowdown; a few parties describe losing the tread briefly among downed timber and having to scramble back onto it. At about mile 6.1 a signed spur splits off to Fern Lake (Trail #1436) — stay on #1437. Around mile 7, at roughly 5,800 ft, the main trail bends sharply east and climbs switchbacks for about a half mile to a junction with the Pyramid Mountain Trail #1433 at about 6,600 ft, roughly a mile southwest of Cardinal's summit and a useful timing landmark. The final approach mile above this junction is noted as steep and loose underfoot. From the open meadow/basin past the junction, leave the trail and hike east through sparse forest, then talus, toward Cardinal's west/southwest flank. For the Southeast Slop
wa_cardinal_peak_se_slopes.descent_text: This is a walk-down/downclimb — no rope work or anchors are needed on the Southeast Slopes line. Reverse the ascent: downclimb the loose scree gully from the notch back into the upper basin, then pick your way back down through talus and sparse forest to rejoin the North Fork Entiat Trail near the Pyramid Mountain Trail junction (~6,600 ft). From there it's a straightforward trail descent down the switchbacks to about 5,800 ft and out along the gentle lower six-plus miles back to the North Fork Entiat Trailhead. The scree gully is the main descent hazard — it's loose top to bottom, so descend deliberately, keep the group tight, and stay alert for rockfall triggered by climbers above. One trip report on this peak noted the descent taking roughly half the time of the ascent once back on established trail. No rappels are required on this route.
wa_cardinal_peak_se_slopes.name: Southeast Slopes

wa_cashmere_mountain_west_ridge.approach: From the Eightmile Lake Trailhead (~3,300 ft, reached via Icicle Creek Road and Road 7601/Eightmile Road as in the drive note), start on the Eightmile Lake Trail (Trail #1552). The trail climbs through partly burned forest and brushy slopes for about 2.8 miles to a junction just past Little Eightmile Lake (~4,400 ft) — this is the last easy water before the high country. At the junction, branch right (north) onto the Eightmile–Trout Creek Trail (Trail #1554), signed toward Lake Caroline. Follow this roughly 2.25–2.75 miles to Lake Caroline, then continue about 0.5 mile to Little Lake Caroline; both lakes sit inside the Enchantments Permit Area, so a permit is required for any overnight camping here. From Little Lake Caroline, continue about 0.8 mile toward Windy Pass (~7,220 ft). Around 6,850 ft, leave the maintained trail and head cross-country to the east, climbing gently; good bivy/camp options appear about 0.5 mile and 250 vertical feet later, around 7,100 ft — this is the last reliable water and the usual high camp for a two-day trip (strong parties push it in a single long car-to-car day, reported at up to ~17 miles round trip). From camp, climb NNE to the broad col on the we
wa_cashmere_mountain_west_ridge.descent_text: Descend by reversing the West Ridge exactly as ascended: downclimb the northwest-facing summit gully back to the ~8,200 ft contour, follow the ridge back down through the same notches/gendarmes to the 8,000 ft west col, then drop SSW back to the ~7,100 ft camp/cross-country section and rejoin the Trail #1554/Windy Pass trail. From there retrace the Eightmile–Trout Creek Trail past Lake Caroline and Little Eightmile Lake back onto Trail #1552 to the Eightmile Lake Trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappels are used on the standard West Ridge route; every description of this line treats it as a reversal of the ascent. The class 3–4 sections are the main descent hazard: the ridge's loose, blocky rock and exposed ledges are more consequential to downclimb than to ascend, and it's easy to drift onto the wrong (steeper) side of the crest while trying to retrace the weaving north/south line through the notches — many parties downclimb the steepest short sections (roughly the last 50 ft below each notch) facing in, one at a time. Afternoon thunderstorm exposure on the long, open ridge and glissade-able but firm early-season snow near Windy Pass are the other things to plan around
wa_cashmere_mountain_west_ridge.name: West Ridge

wa_castle_peak_pasayten_scramble.approach: This route starts with a boat crossing of Ross Lake (Ross Lake Resort water taxi, or a private/inflatable boat carried in via the 0.6-mile portage trail from the SR-20 pullout), landing at the Lightning Creek Trailhead near the head of the lake at roughly 1,500 ft. From the shoreline, follow the Lightning Creek Trail north; parties with their own boat commonly start pre-dawn (around 4am) to leave enough daylight for the long day above, while the water taxi runs only from 8am to 5pm. After about 2 hours of hiking, watch for the junction with the old, no-longer-maintained Freezeout Creek Trail. The first stretch above the junction is the trickiest routefinding on the whole approach: steep rock-and-alder slopes that require a rising, diagonal ascent line before you regain proper forest and trail tread — recent parties note intermittent orange flagging tape marking this stretch, which is worth watching for. Once back in the trees, tread on the Freezeout Creek Trail improves to 'decent shape' as you climb to the Freezeout Cabin at about 3,600 ft, sited immediately after a creek crossing; the cabin (maintained bunks, wood stove, logbook) is a good psychological waypoint and emergency she
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_scramble.descent_text: There is no rappelling on this route — it is a walk-off/downclimb descent that simply reverses the ascent line. From the summit, downclimb the class 2-3 ground back to the notch on the southwest ridge at ~7,600 ft, then descend the same steep heather/talus/scree slope back into the Freezeout Creek drainage. This is the point where parties get into trouble: the upper basin has several gullies and chutes that look similar from above, and dropping into the wrong one risks cliffing out on bluffs well above the creek — stick to the exact ascent gully rather than improvising a shortcut. Cross back to the west side of Freezeout Creek at about 5,000 ft, follow the creek down through the old burn, rejoin the Freezeout Creek Trail tread around 4,200 ft, pass back through the cabin at 3,600 ft, and continue down to the abandoned lower Freezeout Creek Trail / Lightning Creek Trail junction, watching again for the flagged diagonal line through the steep rock-and-alder section. Finish on the Lightning Creek Trail back to the Ross Lake shoreline for the return boat/water-taxi pickup. wa_castle_peak_pasayten_scramble.name: Standard Scramble

wa_castle_peak_pasayten_the_drawbridge.approach: The lawful approach is from the US side: cross Ross Lake by boat, follow the Lightning Creek trail and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail, then work round to the glacier below the north face. The first-ascent party instead came in from Canada — from Lightning Lake in Manning Provincial Park, BC, up and over Frosty Mountain, into Princess Creek basin, across the Princess/Crow Creek divide and down into the Crow Creek drainage — but walking into the US away from a port of entry is not a lawful crossing. On that line the first-ascent party camped on the only dry spot on the ridge, about two-thirds of the way down to the approach glacier.
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_the_drawbridge.descent_text: Descend the south side of the peak and the East Ridge back toward camp; the first-ascent party described this walk-off as straightforward ('breezy'), regaining camp near twilight.
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_the_drawbridge.name: The Drawbridge

wa_north_face_left_buttress.approach: Two approaches exist, both multi-day. The first-ascent party came from Canada: from Lightning Lake in E.C. Manning Provincial Park, about seven miles of trail over the Frosty Mountain area to a pass near 8,000 ft, then cross-country south over the border, through the Princess Creek basin and into the Crow Creek drainage below Castle's north face to the toe of the north-face glacier. Walking into the US away from a port of entry is not a lawful crossing, so that line is recorded, not recommended. The lawful approach is from the US side: boat or hike up Ross Lake from the WA-20/Ross Dam trailhead (permit from the North Cascades Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount) to Lightning Creek, then follow the Lightning Creek Trail and the abandoned, increasingly brushy Freezeout Creek Trail past the Freezeout cabin (3,600 ft), a much longer multi-day trudge. Both approaches finish by crossing the mellow north-face glacier to the base of the buttress -- watch for an awkward bergschrund/moat at the start of the route.
wa_north_face_left_buttress.descent_text: From the top of the route, descend via Castle Peak's east ridge to an obvious col, then down a snow finger back toward the approach glacier/basin, rather than reversing the climbing line.
wa_north_face_left_buttress.name: Fight or Flight
